definition: The central core of some animal fibers, made of loosely packed cells and air spaces, found in coarse wool, many hair fibers and kemp but usually absent from fine wool.
explanation: Inside the cortex of certain fibers runs a medulla, a network of hollow, air-filled cell walls that may be continuous, interrupted or fragmented, and that in some cases collapses into a hollow tube. Medullated fibers tend to be coarser and less dense than unmedullated fibers. The many air and protein interfaces scatter light, so heavily medullated fibers look chalky white and stand out against dyed neighbors. Kemp is a short, thick, brittle fiber type in which the medulla fills most of the width; its stiffness makes it prickly, and manufacturers treat highly medullated fibers as a quality problem in apparel wool.
example: A mill dyes a navy knit from a crossbred wool lot and finds scattered pale, stiff fibers on the fabric face. Testing the retained raw wool reveals a small percentage of heavily medullated fibers. The class traces the fault back to raw material selection and notes that, in dark shades, even a few objectionable fibers per ten thousand can be visible, which is why medullation is tested before purchase.
caution: A medulla is not automatically a defect. Medullation is common in alpaca and llama fleeces, where researchers distinguish visually objectionable from non-objectionable medullated fibers. A medulla also does not identify a species on its own. Keep kemp and guard hair distinct: guard hair describes a coat's coarse outer fibers, while kemp is a highly medullated, brittle fiber. The medulla of animal fibers is also unrelated to the lumen of plant fibers.
deeper: In kemp, the medulla occupies more than about 60% of the fiber diameter. Because medullated fibers contain air, they are less dense than solid fibers, and the refractive mismatch at air and keratin boundaries raises light reflection, producing the chalky look. Measurement methods include projection microscopy, in which medullated fibers are classified and counted while diameters are measured (IWTO-8, with ISO 2647:1973 as the ISO method for wool), and IWTO-57, which determines medullated fiber content from opacity measured on an OFDA instrument. Demand for rapid methods came partly from the South African mohair industry, which needed to detect objectionable medullated fibers at a few per 10,000, and from New Zealand crossbred wool assessment.
origins: Medulla is Latin for marrow or pith, the same word applied to bone marrow and to the soft center of plant stems, and it was extended to the fiber core by analogy. Wool classers and carpet makers have long dealt with kemp and medullated fibers. Standardized measurement took shape with the ISO projection microscope method published in 1973, and later international round trials led to IWTO-57, which uses optical fiber diameter analyzers to measure medullation more rapidly.

definition: Melt spinning makes synthetic filaments by melting a thermoplastic polymer, extruding it through a spinneret, cooling the jets into solid filaments and drawing them to align the molecules.
explanation: Polymer chips or a continuous melt pass through an extruder and a metering pump, are filtered, and are forced through a spinneret plate with many fine holes. The emerging jets are quenched by cross-flowing air, solidify within a short distance, and are wound up or sent straight to drawing rolls. Because no solvent is needed, the route suits polymers that melt without decomposing, including polyester, nylon and polypropylene. Hole shape sets the cross-section (round, trilobal, hollow), and combining two melt streams in one hole produces bicomponent fibers.
example: Two polyester yarns come from the same polymer. One is wound slowly and drawn afterward to several times its length; the other is wound at high speed as partially oriented yarn for later draw-texturing. In a lab tensile test, the undrawn sample stretches easily and breaks at low load, while the drawn one is strong with little extension: processing, not chemistry, created much of the difference.
caution: Melt spinning cannot be used for cellulose, acrylic or para-aramid, which degrade before they melt; those need solution spinning. The spinneret hole diameter does not equal the final filament size, because the jet is thinned by draw-down and later drawing. 'Melt-spun' also says nothing about recycled content, dyeing method or fabric performance.
deeper: Flow through the spinneret capillary is a shear flow that partly orients the chains; on exit, stored elastic energy relaxes and the jet swells (die swell) before being drawn down. Orientation and crystallization then develop along the spinline as the filament cools under tension. Mechanical drawing, from about two times upward, is defined by the draw ratio, the fiber speed after drawing divided by the speed after extrusion; it aligns chains along the fiber axis, raising tenacity and modulus and reducing elongation. Winding at high speed gives partially oriented yarn directly. Semicrystalline polymers such as polyamides and polyesters need this oriented structure to reach useful tenacity.
origins: Melt spinning became an industrial fiber route with the synthetic polymers of the mid-twentieth century, beginning with nylon at DuPont, where Wallace Carothers' research group developed polyamides that could be drawn into strong fibers. The spinneret itself was older, having already been used to extrude solutions in early artificial silk production. Polyester and polypropylene fibers later followed the same basic melt route.

definition: Mercerization treats cotton or other cellulose with concentrated sodium hydroxide, usually under tension, swelling the fibers so they become rounder, more lustrous, stronger and more receptive to dye.
explanation: When cotton meets strong caustic soda, the fibers swell and untwist, and their collapsed, kidney-bean cross-section becomes nearly circular. If the yarn or fabric is held at length or stretched while the alkali is washed out, the swollen form is set in a smooth, rounded shape that reflects light more evenly and gives a silky luster. Without tension the material shrinks strongly and gains dye affinity and strength but little luster, a variant called slack mercerization. The alkali is then rinsed out and neutralized.
example: A thread maker processes two lots of the same combed cotton yarn. The lot mercerized under tension comes out visibly brighter and smoother and dyes to a deeper shade in the same dyebath; the untreated lot looks matte and lighter. To match shades, the mill can use less dye on the mercerized lot, one practical reason to mercerize before dyeing.
caution: Mercerized is a process claim, not a fiber content claim, and does not imply silk or a synthetic blend. Luster also depends on preparation: mercerized yarns are usually combed and often singed, so appearance reflects more than the caustic step. The process uses concentrated alkali and much wash water, so it is not low-impact by default. The change in crystal form is permanent and does not wash out.
deeper: Conventional mercerizing uses roughly 20 to 26 percent sodium hydroxide by mass, traditionally cold (about 0 to 5 C), while hot mercerizing gives better penetration and more even treatment. The alkali penetrates crystalline regions and converts native cellulose I into cellulose II, the stable form after drying, with more accessible hydroxyl groups. Reported benefits include luster, higher tensile strength, greater moisture absorbency, better color yield and higher chemical reactivity. The degree of mercerization is commonly assessed with the barium activity number, which compares the barium hydroxide uptake of treated cotton with that of untreated cotton; higher values indicate more complete treatment.
origins: John Mercer, a chemist and calico printer of Great Harwood, Lancashire, observed the effect of caustic soda on cotton in 1844 and patented the treatment in 1850, valuing the added strength and dye affinity despite heavy shrinkage. Luster came later: Horace A. Lowe patented treatment under tension in 1889, with a further patent in 1890, but let his patents lapse. Commercial interest grew after Thomas and Prevost patented a similar process in 1895.
